                    ### Question
                    A 72-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of blurry vision for the past 3 days. He has also had 4 episodes of right-sided headaches over the past month. He has no significant past medical history. His father died of coronary artery disease at the age of 62 years. His temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 94/min, and blood pressure is 232/128 mm Hg. Fundoscopy shows right-sided optic disc blurring and retinal hemorrhages. A medication is given immediately. Five minutes later, his pulse is 75/min and blood pressure is 190/105 mm Hg. Which of the following drugs was most likely administered?

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The 72-year-old man presents with blurry vision, headaches, and severely elevated blood pressure (232/128 mm Hg), indicating a possible hypertensive emergency with risk of end-organ damage, as evidenced by optic disc blurring and retinal hemorrhages. Immediate medication is required to lower blood pressure rapidly. Labetalol and Nitroprusside are both effective for acute blood pressure control in emergencies. Labetalol is commonly used due to its dual action as an alpha and beta blocker, while Nitroprusside is a potent vasodilator that provides rapid blood pressure reduction. The observed decrease in pulse and blood pressure after medication suggests effective treatment. Although Hydralazine, Nicardipine, and Fenoldopam can be used for hypertension, they are not first-line choices for immediate control in hypertensive emergencies. Therefore, the most likely medication administered is Nitroprusside, given its rapid action and effectiveness in such scenarios.
